Descry
de-SKRY
verb
From Old French descrier, “to cry out, proclaim, announce,” hence to spy out and give report of; some trace a blending with descrire (to describe). In the KJV it is the single-verse rendering of Hebrew tūr / the sense of spying out and reconnoitring a place.

Biblical Definition

To descry is to spy out, to reconnoitre, to catch sight of and report—the scout’s work of discovering a place before the host moves against it. The word stands but once in the whole KJV: the house of Joseph sent to descry Bethel (Jdg 1:23), sending men to spy out the city (once called Luz) before taking it, and the spies’ kindness to an informer opened the gate. Rare as the verb is, the deed it names runs through the Scriptures like a thread. The LORD Himself commands the reconnaissance of the promised land: Send thou men, that they may search the land of Canaan (Num 13:2), and Moses sent them to spy out the land of Canaan (Num 13:17)—a descrying that ended in unbelief when ten of the twelve saw giants and forgot the promise. Joshua later sent out of Shittim two men to spy secretly (Jos 2:1), and their descrying of Jericho met the faith of Rahab, whose scarlet line and confession saved her house. So the descrier’s errand is neither idle nor faithless in itself; the sin at Kadesh was not the spying but the seeing without faith, measuring the giants and not the God who gave the land. To descry rightly is to reconnoitre the field of obedience with the eye of faith—to see the walls and the giants truly, and the LORD more truly still, going up at once because He that promised is able.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines DESCRY as to espy; to explore; to examine by the eye; to detect or discover something distant or concealed.

expand to see more

DESCRY, v.t. — To espy; to detect; to discover at a distance something before hidden or not clearly seen. The house of Joseph sent to descry Bethel (Jdg 1:23).

DESCRY, v.t. — To explore; to examine and view, as a scout or spy who reconnoitres a place before an army advances.

DESCRY, v.t. — To discover or perceive, as an object dimly seen or partly concealed; to make out with the eye.

DESCRY, n. — Discovery; a thing descried; the sight or detection of what was distant or hidden.

DESCRIER, n. — One who descries, espies, or discovers; a scout or discoverer.

Key Scripture

Jdg 1:23 — "And the house of Joseph sent to descry Bethel. (Now the name of the city before was Luz.)"

Num 13:2 — "Send thou men, that they may search the land of Canaan, which I give unto the children of Israel: of every tribe of their fathers shall ye send a man, every one a ruler among them."

Num 13:17 — "And Moses sent them to spy out the land of Canaan, and said unto them, Get you up this way southward, and go up into the mountain:"

Jos 2:1 — "And Joshua the son of Nun sent out of Shittim two men to spy secretly, saying, Go view the land, even Jericho. And they went, and came into an harlot's house, named Rahab, and lodged there."

Modern Corruption

A KJV hapax, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the difference between reconnoitring the field of obedience with the eye of faith and the faithless seeing that measures the giants and forgets the God who gave the land.

expand to see more

The temptation the word rebukes is the sin of the ten spies—to descry the land and see only the giants. The men sent to spy out Canaan reported truly of the walled cities and the sons of Anak, and their true report became a lie because it left God out of the reckoning. This is the abiding snare of the anxious heart: to survey the obstacles of obedience with an accurate eye and a faithless one, to count the difficulties and never the promises, and so to melt the courage of the whole camp. Caleb and Joshua descried the same giants and said, Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able. The difference was not in the eyes but in the faith behind them. To descry rightly is to see the field truly, giants and all, and the LORD who gave it more truly still.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is faith’s reconnaissance—the sober counting of the cost that Christ enjoins, joined to the confident reckoning of the God who cannot fail. The house of Joseph descried Bethel and took it; Joshua’s spies descried Jericho and found Rahab’s faith already at work behind the walls; and the LORD Himself commanded the searching of the land He had already given. There is no virtue in a blind venture, and none in a faithless survey. Look before you go up—and then, having seen the giants, go up at once, because He that promised is able to perform.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old French descrier (to cry out, proclaim, spy out) — to espy, reconnoitre, discover; the KJV hapax at Jdg 1:23, kin to the spying out of the land in Numbers and Joshua.

expand to see more

Old French descrier — to cry out, proclaim, and hence to spy out and give report; the source of English descry.

Latin quiritare / discria- — underlying the sense of raising a cry, from which the notion of announcing a discovery derives.

Hebrew tūr (H8446) — to spy out, explore, search out (Num 13:2, 17, of searching the land of Canaan).

Hebrew rāgal (H7270) — to go about on foot as a spy, to reconnoitre (Jos 2:1, Joshua’s two men spying Jericho).

English describe — a near cousin through the same field of proclaiming and setting forth what is seen.

Usage

"The house of Joseph sent to descry Bethel—the KJV’s single use of the verb, the scouts’ work of spying out a city before the host went up."

"The ten spies descried the land and saw only the giants; Caleb and Joshua descried the same giants and said, we are well able—the difference lay not in the eyes but in the faith behind them."

"Joshua’s two men descried Jericho and found Rahab’s faith already at work; the descrier’s errand met the scarlet line that saved a house."
